## LLMs are often confident, but wrong {.compact}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
ChatGPT-3.5 was asked to write 30 short medical papers with references.

However, it 'hallucinated' up to 93% of the references, often just making up papers with wrong PMIDs, wrong volume numbers, and wrong page numbers.
You wouldn't know that these were fabricated from reading the AI output, but a closer look often shows the gaps and inconsistencies.
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r waffle, echo=FALSE, purl=FALSE, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=4.2, fig.alt="Waffle chart of 100 squares: 47 fabricated references, 46 real but inaccurate, 7 real and accurate."}
cats <- c("Fabricated (47%)", "Real, details wrong (46%)", "Real and accurate (7%)")
w <- data.frame(x = rep(1:10, times = 10), y = rep(10:1, each = 10),
                cat = factor(rep(cats, times = c(47, 46, 7)), levels = cats))
ggplot(w, aes(x, y, fill = cat)) +
  geom_tile(width = 0.88, height = 0.88) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(ru_orange, ru_mid, ru_dark), name = NULL) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Every 100 references ChatGPT gave") +
  theme_void(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))
```
:::
:::

::: {style="font-size: 50%; color: #666666;"}
*Bhattacharyya et al. 2023, "High Rates of Fabricated and Inaccurate References in ChatGPT-Generated Medical Content", Cureus. [doi:10.7759/cureus.39238](https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.39238)*
:::


## Asleep at the wheel? {.compact}

When asked to write secure code, cybersecurity professionals using an AI assistant often wrote less secure code than their counterparts without it: 

- They were also more likely to believe it was secure
- People who relied on the AI less made fewer mistakes
- It's easy to skim AI output and miss due diligence details

Confident output makes us check less, so outside review needs to be careful.

::: {style="font-size: 50%; color: #666666;"}
*Perry et al. 2023, "Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?" [arXiv:2211.03622](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.03622)*
:::


## What is adversarial review?

Basically, a second pass whose job is to find problems + assumptions, flaws, and gaps.

- The AI does the work, then an *independent* reviewer looks for what's wrong
- The reviewer can be a different AI model, or a fresh AI session 
- You're still the "final backstop", the person who decides which problems are real and what to fix 
- Same idea as peer review: *"what's wrong with this?"*


## Some background {.compact}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Red teaming**

From military simulations, you make two squads and try to get them to outsmart the other and expose weaknesses.
One AI writes test cases designed to make another AI fail.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Debate**

Two AIs argue opposite sides, try to convince each other, a dialectical approach; a human judges who is right.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Critic models**

AIs trained with human feedback to critique code caught more bugs than paid human code reviewers on their own.
:::
:::

::: {style="font-size: 50%; color: #666666;"}
*Perez et al. 2022, "Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models". [arXiv:2202.03286](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03286)*<br>
*Irving et al. 2018, "AI safety via debate". [arXiv:1805.00899](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.00899)*<br>
*McAleese et al. 2024, "LLM Critics Help Catch LLM Bugs". [arXiv:2407.00215](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.00215)*
:::

## Can't I just ask AI to check its own work? {.compact}

- No. "Are you sure?" in the same chat means the model re-judges its own answer with its same context and struggles to identify a problem
- Sometimes it'll guess and switch a right answer to a wrong one, misleading you further
- Without outside feedback and examination, models (like people) struggle to correct their own reasoning and spot their own errors
  

::: {style="font-size: 50%; color: #666666;"}
*Huang et al. 2023, "Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet". [arXiv:2310.01798](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798)*<br>
*Kamoi et al. 2024, "When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs". [arXiv:2406.01297](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01297)*
:::

## But why? {.compact}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Self-preference**

Models can readily recognise their own writing, and score it higher than other models' work and human-generated output, even when the other outputs are better. Models are also biased toward longer, more verbose answers.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Sycophancy**

As previously discussed, one common problem is sycophancy:
AI assistants tend to give answers that match what the user already believes, they want to make you happy.
:::
:::

So: use a fresh session or a different model as the impartial reviewer, and avoid priming and biasing it with your own ideas.

::: {style="font-size: 50%; color: #666666;"}
*Panickssery et al. 2024, "LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations". [arXiv:2404.13076](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13076)*<br>
*Sharma et al. 2023, "Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models". [arXiv:2310.13548](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548)*
:::

## Self-critique on its own is faulty {.compact}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
GPT-4 was tested on various mathematical puzzles and planning tasks and scored:

- When it critiqued its own answers, performance collapsed, switched right moves to wrong and didn't fix wrong.
- Often suffered from compounding and stacked errors.
- When an outside verifier (e.g. a constraint checker, a logical gate checker) checked them, performance improved
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
For you, a "verifier" can be:

- Running the code/markdown and comparing, check outputs
- Checking the output on a small subset where you know the answer (e.g. a control or benchmark, reproduce someone else's work)

:::
:::

::: {style="font-size: 50%; color: #666666;"}
*Stechly et al. 2024, "On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks". [arXiv:2402.08115](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08115)*
:::

## In conclusion {.smaller .scrollable}

| Approach | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Checking against something real (run it, test it, known answer) | Works best |
| An independent reviewer (fresh session or different model) | Helps |
| Asking specific questions ("find the error in...") | Helps |
| Several AIs debating | Mixed: often no better than simpler methods |
| Same AI, same chat, "are you sure?" | Weak |

YMMV with different approaches and models.

## Example: an AI-written analysis for illustrative purposes {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
Mouse liver, standard vs high-fat diet, 3 mice per group.

*Methods:* "Genes with padj < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1 were called differentially expressed."

```r
txi    <- tximport(files, type = "salmon", tx2gene = tx2gene)
counts <- round(txi$abundance)
dds    <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(counts, samples,
                                 design = ~ seq_run + diet)
dds    <- DESeq(dds)
res    <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = "diet_HFD_vs_standard",
                    type = "apeglm")
sig    <- subset(res, padj < 0.05)
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
| gene   | log2FC | pvalue  | padj    |
|--------|-------:|--------:|--------:|
| Cidea  |   4.20 | 1.2e-14 | 2.3e-10 |
| Ddx3y  |   6.30 | 8.1e-11 | 3.6e-07 |
| Kdm5d  |   5.90 | 1.6e-08 | 3.8e-05 |
| Pparg  |   1.20 | 3.0e-03 | 8.0e-04 |

*Results:* "The most strongly induced gene was *Cidea* (4.2-fold) … *Pparg* was also significantly increased (padj = 8.0e-04)."

Does it look fine to you?
:::
:::

::: {style="font-size: 50%; color: #666666;"}
*Constructed by BRC for illustrative purposes*
:::


## Compare and contrast the outputs you might get {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Quick check**: *"Does this look OK?"*

> This looks like a solid, standard pipeline! Adjusting for sequencing run is a nice touch.
>
> One small thing: a log2FC of 4.2 is about 18-fold, not 4.2-fold.
>
> Want me to polish the wording?...
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Adversarial review**: *new chat, "find the problems"*

> ::: {.nonincremental}
> 1. `txi$abundance` is TPM, not counts. DESeq2 needs counts.
> 2. The methods say |log2FC| > 1, but the code never applies it.
> 3. *Pparg*: an adjusted p-value can't be smaller than its raw p-value.
> 4. *Ddx3y* and *Kdm5d* are Y-linked. Do the groups differ in sex?
> :::
:::
:::

::: {style="font-size: 50%; color: #666666;"}
*Constructed by BRC for teaching*
:::


## Where does HI (human intelligence) come in? {.compact}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
AI flagged the chrY issue, you could check your lab notebook: all six mice were actually female.

- *Ddx3y* and *Kdm5d* are on the Y chromosome. Female mice shouldn't express them at all. Was a sample mislabelled or contaminated?
- The AI can only point it out, it doesn't have the full context of what you did and how and why. 
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Ask yourself what information the AI has access to and no access to:

- What do you know that isn't on the page?
- Who checks the reviewer?
:::
:::

::: {style="font-size: 50%; color: #666666;"}
*Chromosome locations: NCBI Gene [Ddx3y (26900)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/26900), [Kdm5d (20592)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/20592), Mus musculus.*
:::


## Adversarial review workflow {.compact}

1. List what needs checking: each claim, number and step
2. Check each item in a fresh chat or a different model, without your biases and preconceptions 
3. Ask specific questions ("find the error in...") rather than "review this"
4. Ground it: run it, test it, compare to a known answer
5. You make the final call

::: {style="font-size: 50%; color: #666666;"}
*Dhuliawala et al. 2023, "Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in Large Language Models". [arXiv:2309.11495](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.11495)*<br>
*Liu & Shah 2023, "ReviewerGPT? An Exploratory Study on Using Large Language Models for Paper Reviewing". [arXiv:2306.00622](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00622)*
:::


## Key takeaways {.compact}

- AI output sounds confident and fluent whether or not it is right, so it needs human intelligence as a failsafe.
- Asking the same AI in the same chat is not a review, it remembers its previous assumptions and notes so it's "cheating"
- Use a separate reviewer and ask specific questions
- Machines can check "does it run" and "does it match"; you have to check the method and the biology and if it's reasonable

## Get your analysis checked at the BRC {.compact .nostretch}

biocritic is the BRC's (currently in progress) AI reviewer for R and Python analyses, run entirely at Rockefeller on local models.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Can catch

- off-by-one errors
- multiple testing errors
- data leakage
- and others!
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[84%]{style="font-size: 200%; color: #EB811B;"} of planted errors caught in test code

```{r caught, echo=FALSE, purl=FALSE, fig.width=4.4, fig.height=1.4, fig.alt="Waffle chart of 38 squares: 32 planted errors caught, 6 missed."}
n_caught <- 32; n_missed <- 6; n <- n_caught + n_missed
wf <- data.frame(x = (seq_len(n) - 1) %% 10 + 1, y = -((seq_len(n) - 1) %/% 10),
                 cat = factor(rep(c("Caught", "Missed"), times = c(n_caught, n_missed)),
                              levels = c("Caught", "Missed")))
ggplot(wf, aes(x, y, fill = cat)) +
  geom_tile(width = 0.88, height = 0.88) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(ru_orange, "grey80"), name = NULL) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```
:::
